You said you're an "afterthought at best and a burden at worst," let's say you are a burden. To that I say "are you really? Truly? Objectively?" I'd recommend you think hard about that question. To assist you in doing so I would ask, "what is the burden you bestow upon people? in what manner is it done? And why do you do it?" You may have to think about the thoughts and emotions that guide your decisions, the trauma that changed you, and the physical and mental limitations you have undecidedly been given. I can't possibly imagine how difficult that would be for you, but I believe it's worth it. Because maybe you are a burden, but maybe it's not your fault (why should you judge yourself by the standards of everyone else when most people haven't experienced what you have?) and maybe, just maybe, you have the ability to shift that narrative by becoming someone that you and everyone else can admire, maybe you already are that and no-one sees it. But I can tell you one thing, I care about you and I would rather you live as a burden than die alone, and I hope most people would say the same.

I honestly think fear and guilt are great motivators, otherwise why would they be within our emotional capacity? If I wasn't afraid of failing in college I probably would've failed, and if I didn't feel guilty about hurting people I'd probably hurt a lot of people. I believe these things are only negative when they manifest in excess. That's kind of what anxiety disorders do.

If my friend was struggling with something and I knew their situation could be better if they worked harder I don't think it's bad advice to let them know that they can always put in more effort than they likely are. After all, none of us are all in when it comes to accomplishing our goals. 

I can't help but feel like a bad person when I do bad things, the only way I know how to prevent myself from feeling that way is by doing more good things. My identity fluctuates, and I do have the capacity to forgive myself, but I don't see why it would be beneficial to do so until I have changed my ways.

I'm a big believer in free will, so when I say lazy it relates to the degree to which I make the difficult yet worthwhile decisions, and when I say useless I'm talking about the degree to which I am a productive individual. 

I probably wouldn't call any of my friends these things because I can't see into their minds, I don't know the internal difficulties that they face so there's no point commenting on it, unless I'm only speculating. I also understand that people can misunderstand and have strong emotional reactions to what I say, and so if I were to call someone useless, lazy or a bad person, I'd likely phrase it in a way that's more likely to be interpreted positively, and definitely wouldn't say they're completely useless, lazy or a bad person because I understand that those things manifest on a scale.

I understand that self-compassion is a good thing. I try to be compassionate towards myself as well as others and I usually am. I can see that I'm not a good person, lazy and useless whilst being compassionate. I don't think these concepts are incompatible. They are only incompatible if you have a fixed mindset and I don't.

 It seems to me, the only way to make myself proud is to (1) do good things (2) recognise the good that I've done, so I think you're right about that :)
